items.headline: Big Tech is now competing with the Treasury for capital
items.summary: On the All-In podcast, Chamath Palihapitiya and David Friedberg estimated that the financing the largest AI spenders need through 2027 could equal roughly 30% of U.S. Treasury issuance. Bill Ackman made a related case separately: he compared pure-play neoclouds to highly levered real-estate developers and expects that heavy competition for debt keeps rates high.

items.headline: The bull reply: judge the spend by its return, not by free cash flow
items.summary: VJN Capital argues Amazon's headline free cash flow hides about $145 billion of trailing growth capex; on its "owner FCF" measure, cash generation grew 36.8%, while the cloud backlog rose 16.5% quarter on quarter and 189% year on year. Bill Ackman says Amazon, Meta and Microsoft now make up about a third of his portfolio.

items.headline: The AI money gets harder to raise: OpenAI cuts its round to about $20 billion
items.summary: OpenAI has lowered the target for its latest funding round from $30 billion to about $20 billion, at a hoped-for valuation of $1.25 trillion, the Financial Times reported. The Wall Street Journal said about $11 billion is secured so far and described investor response as tepid; a UAE group including MGX is the largest participant, and a retail offering is planned. In the same week, Nvidia was reported to be weighing a guarantee of debt for Nscale's West Virginia data center, whose first 460 MW building is tied to a $44.6 billion Anthropic contract.
items.short: OpenAI cuts its round target to ~$20B at $1.25T (FT); WSJ says ~$11B secured. Nvidia weighs guaranteeing Nscale's data-center debt.

items.headline: Intel's weak outlook sets off a global chip rout
items.summary: Intel shares fell about 29% on Friday, on course for the company's worst day ever, after it guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15–16 billion and adjusted earnings to $0.25 a share, well below the $17.1 billion and $0.43 analysts expected. CEO Lip-Bu Tan blamed a severe PC slowdown driven by soaring memory costs and shortages, plus an Israel fab shutdown that could cost about $600 million in revenue over two quarters. Together with worries over Amazon's spending, the warning dragged chip and memory stocks sharply lower.
items.short: Intel down ~29% on Q4 guide of $15–16B vs $17.1B expected; Tan blames PC slump from memory costs and an Israel fab shutdown.

items.author: Rafe Fletcher
items.text:
Only if we still view AI as a language-generation tool. Producing plausible but empty prose is where it is useless. 

So in big businesses it amplifies bureaucracy. When busyness is how you measure utility - pointless meetings, emails etc get drawn out as it proliferates the slop. 

But when you have autonomy and agency, it is fantastic. As a small business owner, I link it into Xero & CRMs, and instantly identify priorities. Embedded into email too, AI understands context and stops days becoming about clearing inboxes & helps focus on what's actually important.

AI reflects our existing structures. And where those structures are superficial, it is pain in the arse. But without those burdens, it's a brilliant leveller and dispenses with a lot of onerous crap.

items.author: Fireside Alpha

Bill Ackman says Neuralink and other brain-computer interfaces will let the blind see again within "not too many years"

“And you know, my daughter, who lost pretty much basic function, ability to walk, ability to speak, ability to see, is regaining function. She’s cognitively, as far as I can tell, fine. She’s relearning how to speak, and she’s learning again how to walk. And I’m confident we’re going to get her back."

"Biggest challenge right now is that the optic nerve damage from the pressure on the brain has caused her to lose probably 98% of her vision."

"But even there I’m optimistic. Spent a lot of time in the last few months meeting with all these brain computer interface companies, obviously Neuralink being the most famous, but there’s some other very promising lower intervention technologies."

"And this will be a period, you know, AI is going to enable us. We’re going to be able to get more signal from the brain, and we’re going to be able to interpret that signal much more effectively than we had before. And the blind will see again, and people who have not been able to walk, so to speak, paraplegics, I believe will walk again. It’s a matter of not months but years, but not too many years.”

items.headline: Neoclouds: locked-in backlog versus spot pricing
items.summary: Daniel argues CoreWeave's bigger issue is the upside it gave up by contracting capacity early: deals signed in early 2026 brought roughly $10–15 million per megawatt, while some premium contracts now reach $50 million. Nebius keeps part of its capacity for higher-priced short-term deals. Financing is the other test: Lambda, with a $50 billion backlog ($35 billion tied to Anthropic), has reportedly cut its pre-money target from $14.5 billion to $13 billion.

items.headline: Memory is now the most profitable business in chips
items.summary: SK Hynix posted an 80% operating margin last quarter on 104.6 trillion won of revenue, above TSMC's 59%; in early 2023 its margin was minus 67%. From Nov. 1 it has a new Americas headquarters led by its HBM chief, Ahn Hyun, alongside a $4 billion packaging plant in Indiana. In Korea, chip startup FuriosaAI raised $620 million at a $2.9 billion valuation, with its next chip planned on 2 nm with HBM4.

items.author: Daniel
items.text:
$AMD will generate more than $100B in annual revenue from server CPUs alone by 2030.

Lisa Su expects the server CPU TAM to reach $220B by 2030, with AMD capturing more than 50% of that market.

And I wouldn’t be surprised if the opportunity turns out to be even bigger.

Just look at how aggressively AMD has raised its server CPU TAM projections for 2030:

• November 2025: $60B
• Q1 2026: $120B
• October 2026: $220B

$60B → $120B → $220B.

50% of $220B = $110B in annual revenue for AMD.

From CPUs alone.

And that doesn’t even include the massive opportunity in GPUs.

For context, AMD generated approximately $41B in total revenue over the last 12 months.

The explosion of AI agents will unleash an unprecedented surge in CPU demand.

AI agents don’t just generate responses. They execute code, interact with applications, process data, and coordinate complex workflows.

As billions of AI agents begin operating autonomously, server CPU demand will explode.

$AMD will be one of the biggest beneficiaries of the agentic AI revolution.

items.headline: The bear case for election week
items.summary: @KevInvestingYT, a self-described AI bull, argues semis could see a sharp but short drop if Democrats sweep Tuesday's midterms. items.headline: An AI-agent hacking campaign hit 200 organizations in 11 days, CrowdStrike says
items.summary: CrowdStrike says a China-linked group used AI agents, running mainly on DeepSeek, to target more than 200 organizations in 14 countries in 11 days, including 19 in the U.S. About 70% were compromised. The agents lifted the attack pace from about 40 commands an hour to more than 1,500, and one intrusion consumed about 1.4 billion tokens.

items.title: Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy
items.author: Patrick Collison
items.summary: Stripe's co-founder argues that companies are the original superintelligence, profiting from consumers' bounded rationality, and that personal AI agents could weaken price discrimination and cross-subsidies while acting as a structural subsidy for product quality. He leaves open whether agents produce superstar effects or more dispersion, and who controls how demand is routed. His tentative conclusion: the rewards for simply making better products may go up.

items.title: OpenAI Understands Something Important and Rare
items.author: David George (a16z)
items.summary: Starting from Drucker's line that the purpose of a business is to create a customer, George walks through four levers: new behavior, distribution, pricing and switching costs. At the model layer switching costs are a Red Queen's race and pricing is competitive, so the durable edge is creating new behavior and owning distribution, where he argues OpenAI leads, with ChatGPT itself a happy accident.

items.title: Building the infrastructure is not the same as capturing the profits
items.author: Rose Celine Investments
items.summary: A three-part thread on why the builders of a technological revolution don't necessarily keep its profits. It separates payback from lifetime return on capital and asks you to count replacement capex, financing costs and the spread between return and cost of capital, using Nebius as the worked example. The question to study is who captures the value, not whether AI is big.

items.title: Is writing quality subjective or objective? 16 lessons
items.author: David Perell with Michael Dean
items.summary: Perell distills a long conversation with Michael Dean into 16 craft lessons: fundamentals come before taste, storytelling stretches the unknown across time, titles do triple duty and boredom is the invisible enemy. Write about less, write the first draft for yourself and the second for the reader, and treat the paragraph as the atomic unit.

items.headline: A 2.8-million-person study maps 48 new Alzheimer's risk regions
items.summary: A genetic study of 2.8 million people, published in Nature, identified 127 regions linked to Alzheimer's risk, 48 of them new, pointing to the brain's immune cells (microglia) as well as neurons as key players.

items.headline: A new lever on LDL cholesterol, so far only in mice
items.summary: A Nature study found that high-cholesterol diets cut liver LDL receptors through a Ral/CTSA pathway; blocking CTSA lowered LDL in mice. Whether it works in people is untested.

items.headline: NASA's Swift telescope is days from falling back to Earth
items.summary: NASA ended the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory's mission on Oct. 20 after its orbit decayed too quickly; a Katalyst Space rescue craft launched in July failed to boost it. Reentry is expected around Nov. 4, with a wide uncertainty window. Most of the 1.5-ton telescope should burn up, though some tungsten and mirror parts may survive.

items.headline: How a common gut bacterium can set up colon cancer
items.summary: Johns Hopkins researchers report in Nature that the toxin from Bacteroides fragilis damages the colon by acting on the protein claudin-4; a decoy molecule protected mice from the toxin's effects.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a card is red on one side, it has a circle on the other.
items.explanation: Red could hide something that breaks the rule; Triangle breaks it if the other side turns out to be Red. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.

items.author: GREG ISENBERG
items.text:
The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere, in your team, your metrics and now your AI agents.

It's basically when you reward people for hitting a number, and they find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse.

The name "Cobra Effect" comes from a story about Delhi under British rule. There were too many cobras in the city, so the government offered a reward for every dead cobra people brought in. 

Instead of hunting them, people started breeding cobras so they could kill them and collect the money! …

Data centers don’t work without power. This is not about promises of power tomorrow. Or forecasted power in 2028. Power TODAY. 

Chips can’t operate profitably unless installed in a functional data center. If you can install chips, it’s because you’ve solved the power problem. …
